docs.text:
Welcome to the manual of the Meshhessen Client — the free Windows client for Meshtastic devices.

docs.title: 🚀 Getting Started & Connection
docs.text: ← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

docs.title: Installation in 5 steps
docs.text:
1. Download: Get the latest MeshhessenClient.exe from Releases — the EXE ships with the complete .NET runtime (self-contained), nothing to install
  2. Connect device: Plug in your Meshtastic device via USB (or have TCP/Bluetooth ready)
  3. Launch: Double-click MeshhessenClient.exe – the app runs directly, no installer
  4. Connect: Select connection type (Serial, TCP, or Bluetooth) → click "Connect"
  5. Start: Wait 3–10 seconds for channels to load, then send messages

Only if you build the client from source do you need the .NET 8 SDK.

The app is fully offline-capable. No cloud, no registration, no telemetry to the developer.

docs.title: ⚠️ Windows SmartScreen
docs.text: On first launch Windows SmartScreen may warn about an "unknown publisher" — normal for unsigned open-source downloads: the EXE is not signed with a (paid) code-signing certificate. "More info" → "Run anyway" starts the app. To be safe, download only from the official GitHub releases and compare the SHA-256 checksum published there (PowerShell: Get-FileHash MeshhessenClient.exe).

docs.title: What the app writes to disk
docs.text: Everything stays in the EXE directory (portable, USB-stick friendly): meshhessen-client.ini (settings), telemetry.db (telemetry), maptiles/ and vectortiles/ (map cache), logs/ (message logs), traceroutes/ (saved traceroutes).

docs.text:

docs.text:

  • Multi-language – German and English (switchable in settings)
  • Dark mode & ModernWPF Fluent design

docs.text:
All messages are logged automatically under [EXE directory]/logs/:

  • Channel_0_Primary.log – channel history
  • DM_DEADBEEF_Alice.log – direct messages

docs.title: 📖 Glossary — Meshtastic terms in a nutshell
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

SNR (signal-to-noise ratio, dB) How far the signal sits above the noise. Thanks to spreading, LoRa decodes signals below the noise floor — depending on the modem preset down to about −7 dB (short presets) or −20 dB (Long Slow). Rule of thumb: > 5 dB very good, around 0 dB solid, clearly negative = marginal. RSSI (received signal strength indicator, dBm) Absolute reception level. Typical LoRa values range from ≈ −60 dBm (very close/strong) to ≈ −125 dBm (reception limit). Unlike SNR it is independent of the noise level — both together tell the story. Noise floor (dBm) Base noise at the receiver (environmental interference + receiver noise). Approximation: RSSI ≈ noise floor + SNR. Newer firmware reports it in LocalStats. Hop

One forward through a relay node (Meshtastic counting: direct = 0 hops). Every hop adds latency and airtime; the hop limit (default 3, max. 7) bounds a message's reach. Not to be confused with the number of radio legs:

Link Hops (relay forwards) Radio legs A → B 0 1 A → R1 → B 1 2 A → R1 → R2 → B 2 3 Airtime The time a transmission occupies the radio channel. A shared resource: the longer the modem preset and the more packets/hops, the less capacity remains for everyone else. Channel utilization (%) Share of time the channel is busy (own + foreign transmissions). Persistently above ~25–40 % gets critical — packets collide and get lost. Modem preset (e.g. Short Slow, Long Fast) Combination of bandwidth and spreading factor. "Short" presets = higher data rate, shorter airtime, less range; "long" presets the other way around. All nodes of a mesh must use the same preset. MQTT Internet bridge between mesh islands: gateways lift packets onto a broker and back. Great for reach — but a "neighbor via MQTT" is not a radio neighbor. That's why the client labels MQTT segments separately. Direct neighbors / real RF neighbors Nodes provably heard directly over radio (0 hops, no MQTT) — proven by own direct reception, traceroute hop pairs or NeighborInfo packets. NeighborInfo Packet type with which a node itself reports whom it hears directly — one of the three evidence sources for real RF neighbors. Traceroute Diagnostic request that records the path to a target node: every station adds itself with per-hop SNR (outbound and return). PKI (public key infrastructure) Key pairs (X25519) for encrypted direct messages and admin access. The client decrypts PKI DMs client-side (AES-256-CCM) and manages known public keys in node_keys.csv. NodeDB A device's node database: every node ever heard, with names, positions, telemetry snapshots. The client loads it on connect and enriches it with its own telemetry history. LocalStats Statistics telemetry of newer firmware: noise floor, RX total/bad/duplicates, TX/relay counters, nodes online. The basis for rates (packets/h) and the radio overlays. precision_bits (position precision) Meshtastic can deliberately coarsen transmitted positions (e.g. 13 bits ≈ ±2.9 km). The client displays and accounts for this blur (for instance in position estimation). Fresnel zone Ellipsoid-shaped space around a radio link's line of sight that must stay largely clear for clean reception (rule of thumb: 60 % of the 1st zone). Terrain poking into it causes extra loss — exactly what the client's elevation profile shows.

docs.title: 🔒 Kiosk / Training Mode
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

For shared stations (club room, training, events):

  • Enable in settings, set a password and choose what gets hidden while locked: tabs (Nodes, Channels, Settings, Info, Tools, Debug), node configuration, remote admin, telemetry dashboard, SOS button, Meshhessen quick-config
  • 🔒 lock in the footer bar to lock/unlock (only shown when kiosk mode is enabled and a password is set); unlock via password, the app always starts locked in kiosk mode
  • The Messages and Map tabs always stay visible — deliberately not lockable, so the station remains usable
  • While locked, admin commands from Virtual Node clients are additionally blocked (regardless of the VNode setting)
  • ⚠️ Protects against accidents, not attacks – the password is stored as a PBKDF2 hash, but anyone who can edit the INI file can disable the mode
  • Forgot the password? Close the client and set KioskModeEnabled=True to False in meshhessen-client.ini (or clear the KioskPasswordHash=… line and set a new one)

docs.text: ← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

docs.title: Map styles & vector map
docs.text:
Which map style shows what?

Style What it shows Best for OSM Standard Classic street map: places, roads, buildings, POIs Everyday use & navigation — the all-rounder OSM Dark Mode The same map in a dark rendering Night operation, radio room / wall monitor, matches the client's dark mode OpenTopoMap Topographic map with contour lines and terrain shading Site and range planning: the terrain between nodes at a glance

All three styles are available on the raster and the vector map alike. The vector map (MapLibre GL) renders them razor-sharp and additionally brings the optional special-purpose layers and 3D terrain: * Vector maps (switchable in settings, raster remains the default): * Razor-sharp at every zoom level (MapLibre GL), much smaller offline data, style updates without a client update * 🚒 Fire service / rescue layer (see below) * Layer selection in the settings and via the 🗂️ button directly on the map; while a layer is off, not a single byte is loaded for it * Automatic offline cache: areas viewed online keep working without internet; plus a vector offline package downloader (federal state / custom bounding box, topo extras and extra layers as opt-in) * Full feature set: node pins, traceroutes, neighbor lines, position tracks and the right-click menu also work on the vector map * ⛰ 3D terrain – a real elevation model (SRTM; DEM coverage up to ~52° N) with hillshading, toggled via the 🗂️ layer popup; Ctrl+drag tilts the map, a north arrow appears while rotated/tilted (click to re-north); areas viewed once keep working offline * Requires the Microsoft WebView2 runtime (pre-installed on Windows 11); without it the client falls back to raster automatically

docs.title: Map modes
docs.text:
Mode Description Coverage Offline (default) Pre-downloaded tiles from the Meshhessen server. No internet required. Germany, Austria & Switzerland (DACH) Online – Meshhessen Server (DACH) Tiles fetched on demand from tile.meshhessenclient.de and stored permanently. All three styles. Germany, Austria & Switzerland (DACH) Online – custom tile server Same, but with your own configured tile URLs; public OSM/OpenTopoMap servers are not allowed here (tile usage policy). depends on server Online – OpenStreetMap (worldwide) Worldwide coverage via tile.openstreetmap.org; standard map only; OSM tile policy compliant. Worldwide

The OSM online mode is intended for areas outside Germany. The OSM tile server is donation-funded – please use sparingly.

docs.title: Downloading tiles (offline use)
docs.text:
✅ Downloading from the Meshhessen server is explicitly encouraged — tile.meshhessenclient.de exists for exactly this purpose; feel free to grab your whole region (be sensible about zoom level and area). Bulk downloads are only blocked from public servers such as OSM/OpenTopoMap — their tile policies forbid them.

  1. Settings → Map / Tiles: select map mode Offline and rendering Raster — the download button is only visible in this combination (the vector map has its own vector-package downloader, see above)
  2. Click "Download Tiles…" — the download dialog opens; you pick the map style right in the dialog:

  1. Define the area: pick a federal state from the list or enter the bounding box manually into the four fields North / South / East / West — Hesse is pre-filled (N 51.7 · S 49.4 · E 10.3 · W 7.8)
  2. Pick zoom levels (min/max fields): up to 12 is enough for an overview, up to 14 (the default) for towns, 15+ only for small areas — every extra level quadruples the tile count
  3. Start the download and watch the progress — existing tiles are skipped, so aborting + restarting is completely harmless
  4. Tiles land under maptiles/, stay available offline permanently and are portable via USB
  5. Don't forget the offline test (see below)

Typical pitfalls:

  • Download refuses to start → public OSM/OpenTopoMap servers are blocked for bulk downloads (tile policy) — use the Meshhessen server or your own tile server
  • Blank areas outside the DACH region → the Meshhessen server covers Germany, Austria and Switzerland; use the OSM online mode (viewing only, no bulk download) elsewhere
  • Download gets huge → lower the zoom cap or shrink the bounding box — going from zoom 14 to 15 alone quadruples the data

How much storage? Rough raster-map figures: Hesse up to zoom 14 ≈ 2–4 GB per map style; all of Germany up to zoom 14 ≈ 20–30 GB. The vector map is far more compact — a vector offline package for a federal state is usually below 1 GB.

⚠️ On SD cards, factor in the allocation unit size (e.g. for the T-Deck): many tiles are only a few hundred bytes but each occupies a full cluster. With the default formatting of large cards (often 128 KB clusters) the real usage multiplies compared to the figures above. Format exFAT with 4096-byte allocation units — the T-Deck assistant recommends and does exactly that.

Offline test: switch the map mode to Offline (or briefly disconnect the network) and pan/zoom through your target region — whatever renders now is genuinely stored locally. Missing tiles show as blank areas; extend the download area/zoom in that case.

docs.title: 🚒 Fire service / rescue layer (vector map)
docs.text:
An optional special-purpose layer for fire services, rescue services and civil protection – meant as support during operations and exercises ("where is the nearest hydrant / rescue point?"). Data comes live from OpenStreetMap (daily updates on the Meshhessen server) – coverage depends on the local mapping state. Colors follow fire-plan conventions: red = extinguishing/alerting, blue = water supply, green = rescue, orange = civil protection. Clicking an object opens a detail popup with all attributes maintained in OSM (type, couplings, flow, pressure, water source, operator, location description, survey date). Icons deliberately overlap ("during an operation you want to see every point"). Works offline for cached areas; while the layer is off, not a single byte is transferred.

The same area as a vector map with the 🚒 fire service / rescue layer enabled (click shows details):

docs.title: 📨 Messaging & Communication
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

  • Send and receive messages (broadcast & direct messages)
  • Multi-channel – all channels from your device loaded automatically
  • Direct Messages (DMs) with a dedicated chat window in a tabbed layout
  • PKI decryption – client-side decryption of PKI-encrypted DMs (X25519 + AES-256-CCM, firmware-accurate); private key is loaded automatically from the connected device
  • Node public key database – local CSV file (node_keys.csv) that the client maintains automatically with the public keys of received nodes (manual edits are read on the next start)
  • Tap-back reactions – react to messages with emoji (32 emojis, like the Android app); right-click a message → emoji picker; works in channel chat and DMs
  • Reply function – reply to individual messages (protocol-level), quoted block with accent-colored highlight
  • Selectable & copyable messages – select text, copy to clipboard, click links; right-click any message → "Copy Message" (always copies the right-clicked message)
  • 🚨 Alert Bell support – send and receive emergency alerts; 🚨 SOS button in chat and DMs; red blinking border + notification bar with "📍 Go to map" button
  • Persistent message database – channel and DM messages in a local SQLite DB (enabled by default; can be turned off in the settings under "Message database")
  • Last 24 hours loaded automatically on connect; older messages lazy-loaded when scrolling up
  • DM history: all conversations from the last 24 h appear automatically when the DM window is opened
  • Per-channel deletion directly in the Channels tab with a time-range dialog (All / 30 / 90 / 365 days)
  • Confirmation before clearing a DM conversation; configurable retention period (30 / 90 / 365 days / unlimited — default: 90 days)

docs.title: How-to: send your first message & an encrypted DM
docs.text:
Goal: send a broadcast into a channel, then an end-to-end encrypted direct message to a specific node.

  1. Channel message: Messages tab → pick the channel in the "Channels" sidebar on the left → type at the bottom → Enter. Your own message shows right-aligned; replies arrive in the same thread
  2. Start a DM: right-click the target node (node list, map, or one of its messages) → "💬 Send DM" — the conversation opens as its own tab in the DM window (or directly in the main window, depending on your settings)
  3. Check encryption: the 🔑 column in the node list shows whether the target's public key is known. 🔑 = PKI DMs can be encrypted and decrypted (X25519 + AES-256-CCM); an empty cell (table) or 🔓 (tile view) means the key is unknown — then only channel encryption applies
  4. Success check: the sent message gets delivery check marks: ✓ = sent, ✓✓ (green) = acknowledged by the recipient (ACK); the reply appears in the tab. Received PKI DMs are decrypted by the client itself
  5. Extras: right-click a message → emoji reaction or "Reply" (quote block); text is selectable and copyable

Typical pitfalls:

  • No 🔑 on the target → the public key is missing locally: receive the node directly once or pull its user info via right-click "📥 Request information → User info" (for encrypted received messages the 🔑 button right on the message works too)
  • No ACK → target currently unreachable (test with a traceroute) or the link is congested — wait briefly instead of resending (airtime!)
  • Old conversation missing → the message database is enabled by default; check whether it was turned off in the settings ("Message database") — without it, history only starts at connect time

docs.title: 📈 Understanding the Values
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

The Meshhessen Client stores all received telemetry data in a local SQLite database and analyses it automatically. Open the analysis window for any node via the node context menu → Telemetry; the LED indicators in the main window give you an at-a-glance overview. This chapter explains what the numbers mean — where to find them in the client is covered in Telemetry & radio analysis.

docs.title: SNR – signal-to-noise ratio
docs.text:
Shows how strong the signal is relative to the noise. Thanks to spreading, LoRa decodes signals below the noise floor – how far depends on the modem preset (short presets ≈ −7 dB, Long Slow down to ≈ −20 dB). The thresholds below are a practical orientation for the presets common around here, not hard limits:

  • 🟢 ▲ > 5 dB – Excellent, stable link
  • 🟢 ● 0 – 5 dB – Good, reliable link
  • 🟡 ● −5 – 0 dB – Marginal, packet loss possible
  • 🔴 ▼ < −5 dB – Poor, frequent packet loss

docs.title: RSSI – received signal strength
docs.text:
Absolute received signal level in dBm. Shows how loud the signal arrives at the receiver regardless of noise. Combined with SNR it gives a complete picture of link quality.

  • 🟢 > −100 dBm – Good
  • 🟡 −100 to −115 dBm – Marginal
  • 🔴 < −115 dBm – Weak

docs.title: Signal trend (regression)
docs.text:
The client calculates the linear trend over the configured time window (default: 6 hours). A negative trend indicates a deteriorating link – e.g. due to changing weather or new obstructions.

  • 🟢 ▲ Rising – Signal improving
  • 🟡 → Stable – No significant trend
  • 🔴 ▼ Falling – Signal deteriorating

docs.title: Battery level (%)
docs.text:
• 🟢 > 50 % – Good
  • 🟡 20 – 50 % – Medium
  • 🔴 < 20 % – Low, charge soon

docs.title: Night-time drop
docs.text:
How many % battery the node consumes overnight (no solar charging). A high night drop indicates elevated idle current or missing deep-sleep configuration.

  • 🟢 < 5 % – Normal (standby current)
  • 🟡 5 – 15 % – Slightly elevated
  • 🔴 > 15 % – Critical, investigate

docs.title: Voltage (V)
docs.text: Raw battery voltage in volts. Typical LiPo values: 4.2 V = fully charged, 3.7 V = nominal, 3.2 V = deep-discharge threshold. Solar nodes show significantly higher voltage during the day.

docs.title: 📡 Channel utilization
docs.text:
Channel utilization shows what percentage of the LoRa time slot on the selected channel is occupied – by the node's own packets and by received packets from other nodes. High channel utilization increases the probability of collisions and packet loss. The Mesh Health tooltip shows the top-5 nodes by channel utilization.

Utilization Rating Recommendation 0 – 10 % 🟢 Excellent Plenty of capacity free, no action needed 10 – 25 % 🟢 Good Normal, healthy mesh 25 – 50 % 🟡 Elevated Reduce position update rate, consider Short Slow preset > 50 % 🔴 Critical Many packet losses expected; reduce telemetry intervals and broadcasts

docs.title: Hop count
docs.text:
How often a packet was forwarded by relay nodes (Meshtastic counting: direct = 0 hops; the number of radio legs is hops + 1). Every forward adds latency and airtime.

  • 🟢 0 hops – Direct link, optimal
  • 🟢 1–2 hops – Normal
  • 🟡 3–5 hops – High, heavy airtime use
  • 🔴 6–7 hops – Maximum, very inefficient

docs.title: Path change rate
docs.text:
How frequently the routing path to a node changes. Frequent path changes indicate unstable intermediate links – e.g. relay nodes at poor locations.

  • 🟢 Stable – Consistent path
  • 🟡 Moderate – Occasional changes
  • 🔴 Unstable – Frequent changes, check relay nodes

docs.title: Hop cost
docs.text: Weighted average hop count over the analysis period. Low hop cost means short, efficient paths; high hop cost increases latency and channel utilization for the entire mesh.

docs.title: 👥 Neighbors
docs.text: Shows all nodes that the selected node hears directly (0 hops, no relay). Per neighbor the SNR of the direct link and its trend over time are displayed. Many stable neighbors indicate good integration into the mesh; few or unstable neighbors indicate range or configuration issues.

docs.title: ⏱️ Airtime
docs.text: Shows how much transmit time (TX airtime) and receive time (RX airtime) the node uses. Nodes with high TX airtime increase channel utilization for all nodes in range. Telemetry intervals and broadcast frequency should be adjusted accordingly.

docs.title: 🔧 "Net:" LED strip – quick reference
docs.text:
The "Net:" strip in the main window rates the whole visible mesh:

LED 🟢 Green 🟡 Yellow 🔴 Red ⚪ Grey Weather/ST (signal weather, short-term SNR trend, 6 h) SNRs stable or rising Slight simultaneous drop Clear simultaneous drop (weather effect) No data LT-SNR (antenna health, 7 days) Long-term trend stable/rising Creeping degradation Falling long-term — check antenna/position No data Nbrs (neighbor quality) ≥ 2 stable neighbors 1 neighbor or declining SNRs No direct links No data Path (route stability) Stable path Occasional changes Frequent path changes No traceroute Mesh Health (score 0–100 %) Good overall state Individual problem areas High channel util. or many unstable nodes No data

docs.title: 🛠️ Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Poor signal (low SNR/RSSI): check antenna for loose connections or damage. Raise the node – clear line of sight significantly extends LoRa range. Keep the antenna vertical. Add a relay node as an intermediate hop.
  • Falling signal trend: monitor weather conditions (moisture and rain attenuate signal). Check outdoor nodes for water ingress in the antenna connector. Verify frequency offset of the node.
  • High channel utilization (> 25 %): switch modem preset to Short Slow (higher data rate via a lower spreading factor = shorter airtime per packet). Reduce position update rate in firmware (e.g. every 10–30 minutes). Increase telemetry intervals (device, environment). Minimize unnecessary broadcasts.
  • Path instability (frequent path changes): identify relay nodes at poor locations using traceroute SNR analysis. Set a fixed position for stationary relay nodes – saves GPS power and stops map positions from jumping (it does not directly control next-hop routing). Analyse the SNR of the affected links via traceroute.
  • High night-time battery drop: review power-saving options per device role: clients/trackers benefit from power saving/deep sleep, routers should stay receive-ready. Reduce display timeout. Check solar panel alignment and cleanliness. Verify charge controller operation.
  • Few or no neighbors: verify channel settings (frequency, modem preset) match neighboring nodes. Improve antenna and node placement. Increase mesh density by deploying another node.

📖 Short definitions of all terms live in the glossary; how to monitor these values as a dashboard is shown in the how-to in the telemetry chapter.

docs.title: 🔧 Node Management & Remote Admin
docs.text: ← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

docs.title: Node overview
docs.text:
• All nodes in the mesh with SNR, battery, distance, hop count
  • Tile view (Fancy View) – optionally enabled in Settings → Appearance: replaces the table with a responsive tile surface (column count grows/shrinks with the window width)
    • Per tile: ShortName badge in node color, 🔑/🔓 PKI status, full name, "X min ago", ⭐ favorite star, 📡 infrastructure and ☁ MQTT icons
    • Power (externally powered or battery + voltage), distance + altitude, hops, RSSI/SNR with color gradient, environment telemetry (🌡/💧/🌬), hardware model · device role · node ID
    • Own node always on top, virtualized scrolling even with 1000+ nodes
  • SNR/RSSI only for direct reception – signal values are shown only when we hear the node directly (0 hops, no MQTT); for relayed nodes the column shows the hop count instead
  • Advanced filters – by "last seen" (5 min to 60 days), hide MQTT nodes, favorites only, SNR coloring on/off; sort dropdown in tile mode
  • Request information – right-click submenu (list, tile, map) requests data from a node like the Android app: user info, position, device/environment/air-quality/power/host metrics, signal quality/mesh stats, PAX counter
  • Node info window – right-click a node (list, tile, map or message) → "ℹ️ Node Info": hardware model, role, PKI status, battery, signal, first/last seen and position. Your own device's firmware version lives under Settings → Device info; a remote node's is shown in the remote admin window:

* PKI key indicator – 🔑 column shows whether a node's public key is known * Node colors – color-code nodes individually (map + lists) * Node notes – free-text annotations per node * Pin nodes – pin nodes to the top of the list (independent of sorting) * Favorites – mark nodes as favorites (★ icon, right-click menu); synced with the device (set_favorite_node / remove_favorite_node); favorites shown at the top of the list

docs.title: Remote administration
docs.text: Full remote admin UI for favorite nodes — also works across relay and MQTT paths:

docs.title: How to administer a remote node (step by step)
docs.text:
1. Prerequisites: your public key must be registered as an admin key on the target node (its security tab, admin keys 1–3) — or you share an admin channel. The target also needs to know your node's public key (PKI).
  2. Mark the target node as a favorite (★ in the right-click menu) — the remote-admin selection dialog only lists favorites
  3. Open "🛠️ Remote Administration" (right-click in the tile view, or Settings → Remote administration) and pick the favorite in the dialog — the client negotiates a session key and loads the configuration (either everything at once or per tab on demand). After the first valid access the target automatically marks your admin node as a favorite, so your key cannot be evicted from its node database
  4. Change settings → "Save" writes them back over the air; the target reboots if required
  5. Typical failures: timeout without a response → admin key missing on the target or the node is currently unreachable (try a traceroute); PKI error → the target's public key is missing locally (receive the node directly once or pull it via "📥 Request information → User info"). Rejections are reported with a concrete reason instead of failing silently.
  6. Across multiple hops every answer takes a few seconds — the timeout is adjustable (default 30 s; 5–300 s live in the window); individual tabs can be retried via "↻ Reload Tab"

Favorites on the remote device can be set/removed remotely, too:

Feature overview:

  • All configuration tabs: Owner, Device, Position, LoRa, Bluetooth, Network, Display, Channels, Security, Control
  • Security tab: public key (read-only, Base64), admin keys 1–3 (Base64), flags (admin channel, managed mode, serial, debug log)
  • Manage favorites remotely: set or remove favorites on the remote device
  • Session-key handshake, configurable timeout, per-channel retry + reload
  • Lazy loading: choose on open whether everything loads immediately or page by page; "↻ Reload Tab" button per tab

docs.title: Node configuration (local)
docs.text:
Full device configuration directly from the client, all modules in one window:

  • Device & LoRa: region, modem preset, TX power, hop limit, device role, rebroadcast mode
  • Position: GPS mode, smart broadcast, fixed position with coordinate input; "Pick from Map" opens a dedicated map picker window; "Own Map Pin" copies the position set via right-click
  • Network: Wi-Fi SSID/PSK, DHCP/static IP, Ethernet, NTP server, syslog
  • Display: screen timeout, carousel, compass, 12h clock, metric/imperial, display mode, OLED type
  • MQTT: server, credentials, TLS, JSON mode, root topic, proxy mode, map reporting with precision level (bits 10–19), MQTT proxy client
  • Telemetry: device, environment, air quality and power metric intervals
  • Bluetooth: enable, pairing mode, fixed PIN; change BT PIN directly from the client
  • Security: show public key (read-only), show/change private key, admin keys, managed mode
  • Channels: all 8 channels – role, name, uplink, downlink, position precision (bits 10–19, ~23 km to ~45 m)
  • Additional modules: neighbor info, store & forward, external notification, canned messages, range test, serial

docs.title: 🔧 T-Deck Map Assistant
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

  • Prepare an SD card – guided 6-step wizard (Tools tab) for loading offline maps onto a Meshtastic T-Deck SD card
  • Step 1 – Welcome: explains the workflow; coverage = Meshhessen tile server (DACH region; the quick picker lists German federal states, the freestyle rectangle also covers Austria/Switzerland)
  • Step 2 – Drive: shows all removable drives with size, free space and file system
  • Step 3 – Formatting: recommends exFAT with 4096-byte allocation units (T-Deck-optimal; small tiles ≈ 100 bytes → small AU saves a lot of space — see the storage notes in "Map & offline use"); formatting via UAC-elevated PowerShell with two confirmations
  • Step 4 – Area: by federal state (checkboxes), all of Germany, or freestyle (one or more rectangles on an interactive map — the enclosing hull is used)
  • Step 5 – Zoom & style: max zoom in fixed steps 8/10/12/14/16/17 (the transfer always starts at zoom 1), warnings from level 14 and 16; OSM / OSM Dark / OpenTopoMap. The wizard estimates tile count and data volume (~15 KB/tile) and warns when the free SD space won't suffice
  • Step 6 – Transfer: additive – SD tile exists → skip; available locally → copy; otherwise → fetch from the tile server + cache locally
  • SD directory structure: {drive}:\maps\OSM\{z}\{x}\{y}.png (T-Deck compatible)
  • ZIP export – export local tiles as a ZIP (filterable by map style)
  • Fully multilingual (German/English)

docs.title: 🏗️ Technology & Protocol
docs.text: ← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

docs.title: Technical overview
docs.text:
Component Technology UI WPF .NET 8, ModernWPF (Fluent) Protocol Meshtastic Protobuf over Serial/TCP/BLE Map Mapsui 4.1 (raster) + MapLibre GL in WebView2 (vector) Serialization Google.Protobuf, System.Text.Json Connection Serial (0x94 0xC3 framing), TCP/WiFi, Bluetooth Low Energy

Connection types:

Type Transport Framing Notes USB/Serial COM port, 115200 baud 4-byte header (0x94 0xC3 + length) Wake-up sequence, debug text interleaved TCP/WiFi TCP socket 4-byte header (same as serial) Configurable hostname/IP + port Bluetooth BLE GATT characteristics Raw protobuf (no framing) Direct FromRadio/ToRadio packets

Connection sequence:

Windows Client → USB/Serial | TCP/WiFi | BLE → Meshtastic Node → LoRa → Mesh
  1. Open connection → send wake-up sequence (Serial/TCP only) → send want_config_id
  2. Receive my_info, node_info (×N), channel (×8), config, config_complete_id
  3. If channels are missing (e.g. T-Deck): retry mechanism up to 3 rounds via GetChannelRequest
  4. Ready for MeshPackets

docs.title: Serial protocol (robustness)
docs.text:
• Max. packet length 512 bytes (per Meshtastic spec), beyond that = corrupt → skip false start
  • Protection against partial header loss (trailing 0x94 byte preserved on buffer clear)
  • Stale-packet timeout: incomplete packets discarded after 5 s
  • Device debug text (ANSI codes) is detected, stripped and logged separately
  • Auto-recovery: sends wake-up + want_config_id if no protobuf packet was received for >60 s

docs.title: Error detection (device logs)
docs.text: Code Description TxWatchdog Software bug while transmitting LoRa NoRadio No LoRa radio found TransmitFailed Radio TX hardware failure Brownout CPU voltage below minimum SX1262Failure SX1262 radio self-test failed FlashCorruptionRecoverable Flash corruption detected (repaired) FlashCorruptionUnrecoverable Flash corruption (unrepairable)

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
Requirements: .NET 8.0 SDK, Windows 10/11 x64

git clone https://github.com/SMLunchen/mh_windowsclient.git
cd mh_windowsclient
git submodule update --init --recursive
dotnet publish MeshhessenClient/MeshhessenClient.csproj -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishSingleFile=true -p:PublishTrimmed=false -o public

The EXE will be at public\MeshhessenClient.exe. Alternatively, run build.bat.

docs.title: 📊 Telemetry & Radio Analysis
docs.text: ← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

docs.title: Telemetry database & dashboard
docs.text:
• Persistent telemetry database – received packet and device data is stored locally in a SQLite database
  • Telemetry Dashboard – freely configurable widget dashboard with named dashboards (📊 button in the toolbar):
  • 14 widget types: line, area, bar, scatter, gauge, stat value, heatmap, histogram, candlestick, state timeline, ranking, multi-stat, mesh health, clock
  • Multi-node support, all metrics: SNR, RSSI, battery, voltage, channel/TX utilization, temperature, humidity, pressure, packets/h, noise floor, RX/TX stats
  • Drag-and-drop arrangement, freely resizable, editable, duplicatable, auto-refresh
  • Zoom/pan on the time axis (survives auto-refresh; double-click resets), day/night shading
  • Warn & alarm zones (Grafana-style): per widget one warning and one alarm bound in each direction; gauge/stat/charts color green/orange/red by zone, Windows toasts report every zone transition (incl. ✅ all-clear)
  • Export: CSV (incl. a German-Excel flavour), widget as PNG, copy image, share whole dashboards as JSON (export/import)
  • Fullscreen mode (F11) for wall monitors; window placement and last active dashboard are remembered
  • Automatic telemetry polling (📥): up to 4 nodes are actively polled for LocalStats/environment/device data (mesh-friendly: LocalStats at most 1×/h, others every 30 min max); counter deltas yield packets/h rates
  • Persisted in dashboards.json, theme-adaptive incl. live Windows theme switching; independent window for a second monitor

📊 Telemetry dashboard – freely configurable widgets with threshold alerts, auto-refresh and fullscreen:

docs.title: How-to: create a dashboard, set an alert, read the values
docs.text:
Goal: a dashboard that watches your solar router's battery and warns you before it runs dry overnight.

  1. Open: 📊 button in the main window toolbar → on first open the window is empty; "+ New" creates your first dashboard (suggested name "Dashboard 1" — call it e.g. "Solar monitoring")
  2. Add a widget: "+ Add Widget" → pick a type (for battery: time series/line), tick the node(s), metric battery (%), range 7 days (the default) → save. On the finished card you can switch via the 1d/7d/14d/30d buttons, reorder via the ⠿ grip and resize via the grip in the lower right
  3. Set the alert: in the widget editor under "Thresholds & alerts" set your bounds — for battery e.g. ⚠ warning low 30 and 🚨 alarm low 15. The lines appear in the chart (orange/red), gauge and stat value color by zone; when the value changes zone on a refresh you get a Windows toast with severity (transition only — no constant nagging; returning to normal reports ✅)
  4. Keep it fresh: auto-refresh top right (e.g. 30 s); if the node rarely sends on its own, add it to the polling plan via the 📥 Polling button (max. 4 nodes, mesh-friendly)
  5. Success check & alert test: the widget shows a curve with day/night shading; the last refresh time is shown at the bottom. Test the alert in two steps: first set the bounds so the current value sits in the normal zone and wait for one refresh — this first check silently records the baseline. Then move a bound past the current value and press "↺ Refresh" (or wait for the auto-refresh): now the toast fires
  6. Reading the values: if the battery drops more than ~15–20 % overnight, see the chapter Understanding the values (night drop, voltage); SNR/RSSI interpretation lives there and in the glossary

Typical pitfalls:

  • Widget stays empty → no data for this node/metric in the telemetry database yet (the node doesn't send that metric → enable polling or right-click "Request information")
  • No toast despite alarm bounds → checks only happen on a refresh (auto-refresh, "↺" or saving in the editor), never while typing — and the very first check after opening silently records the baseline; only the next zone transition is reported. Also check: are Windows notifications allowed for apps?
  • Zoom keeps resetting → zoom/pan survives auto-refresh; the manual "Refresh" button deliberately resets the view

docs.title: 📡 Radio echo: "Who's pinging us?"
docs.text:
Other stations constantly interact with your node without you noticing — they request NodeInfo, position or telemetry, trace the radio path to you or knock on the remote admin. The radio echo makes these invisible requests visible:

  • Radar in the status strip (next to Mesh Health): on a request the little antenna mast emits a colored wave (color = request type, traceroute pulses twice), a counter collects unread events, and a message like "🛰️ KELL is tracing the radio path to us!" appears for a few seconds
  • Click opens the journal: a chronological view of who asked what and when — request bursts from the same station are bundled as ×n, with a source badge (direct / n hops / ☁ MQTT); traceroute requests even show the inbound path ("via …"), telemetry requests the requested data group (environment, power, device metrics …)
  • Statistics tab: requests, stations, traces, "What did the others want to know?" (with a telemetry breakdown by data group) and the most curious node
  • 📡 Curiosity radar (retro sonar): its own tab styled like a classic radar scope — black screen, phosphor-green rings, rotating sweep, your node glowing in the center, the requesting stations around it (the more curious, the closer, bigger and brighter). When a request arrives live, a sonar ping expands from the station to the center and gets "reflected" back. Clicking a station shows hourly request bars and the breakdown
  • Filters: time range (24 h / 7 / 30 days), request type and node search; right-clicking an entry opens node info, map or DM — for traceroute requests the request path can be drawn on the map
  • Response airtime: a statistics tile estimates how much transmit time your node's auto-replies cost (LoRa formula at the current modem preset) — every request also costs your airtime
  • Message style switchable in the settings: casual ("KELL is tracing the path to us!") or factual ("Traceroute request received from KELL"); optional Windows toasts; right-clicking the radar icon toggles 🔕 quiet mode; the feature can be hidden entirely and locked in kiosk mode
  • Honesty: what is detected is the request — whether your node answers is derived from local configuration only, and the journal says so: "✓ reply expected", for position requests including the configured channel precision ("±2.9 km"), "✕ no reply (no position)", "? depends on sensors" or "🔐 only with admin authorization". The actual transmission is invisible to the client; replies to your own requests and overheard packets to third parties deliberately do not show up here
  • Dashboard integration: the metric "📡 radio echo (requests to us/h)" is available as a time series in the telemetry dashboard — including warn/alarm zones

docs.title: Node statistics & real RF neighbors
docs.text:
• Node statistics window – detailed analysis per node:
  • Day/night breakdown of reception quality
  • Time-series graphs for SNR, RSSI, packet rate and device data (battery, voltage)
  • Real RF neighbors – proven by direct reception, traceroute hop pairs and NeighborInfo packets, with SNR in both directions (fills over time; classic "heard" list as automatic fallback until then)
  • LocalStats (newer firmware): noise floor, RX bad/duplicates, TX relay and more (routing tab)
  • "Net:" LED strip in the main window — the state of the whole visible mesh at a glance:
  • Weather/ST – "signal weather": short-term SNR/RSSI trend of all nodes (last 6 h)
  • LT-SNR – antenna health: long-term SNR trend of all nodes (last 7 days)
  • Nbrs – neighbor quality: average link quality to neighbor nodes
  • Path – route stability: frequency of route changes in the mesh
  • Mesh Health – overall score 0–100 % from path costs, route changes, reception rate and channel utilization

docs.title: 📡 Traceroute
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

  • Start traceroute – directly from the node context menu (node list, map, message list)
  • "RF only" mode – sends the request with the OK-to-MQTT bit cleared (pre-encrypted packet): MQTT gateways won't uplink it, the route runs over RF exclusively. Note: the reply may still come back via MQTT — that's up to the target node.
  • Honest MQTT badges: hops only get the MQTT badge when no radio measurement exists for that segment; the header badge "via MQTT" only means "the reply arrived via MQTT"
  • Dedicated window per target node with:
  • Hop table: node name, distance, SNR (in dB), MQTT indicator
  • Live status (waiting / received)
  • ⛰ Elevation profile per hop – right-click a hop row to see the segment's terrain profile (SRTM, line of sight, Fresnel zone)
  • Map plotting – solid line where positions are known, dashed where missing; direction arrows; MQTT bridges as lightning zigzag; click a segment → SNR popup
  • Multiple traceroutes at once on the map – each gets a unique color
  • Save & Load – traceroutes are automatically saved to traceroutes/ as JSON; compare routes over time, load multiple files, load historical traceroutes from the database
  • Time range filter – filter traceroutes by period (3d / 7d / 14d / 30d / 90d / All)
  • Deduplication – show only the latest traceroute per node pair (optional)
  • Map legend – shows all active traces with color and individual ✕ remove button

docs.title: 🖧 Virtual Node – connect phone apps through the PC
docs.text:
← Handbook home · 🇩🇪 Deutsche Version

  • TCP proxy server – connect Meshtastic apps (Android/iOS) to the Meshhessen Client as if it were a real Meshtastic device
  • Configurable in the Tools tab: port (default: 4404), enable/disable, "Block admin commands from clients"
  • Auto-start: the "Enable Virtual Node" checkbox is persisted — the server then starts automatically as soon as a connection to the physical node is established
  • Config replay: connecting apps receive all channels, node list and device config immediately
  • Bidirectional visibility: messages sent in the app appear in connected apps – and vice versa
  • Multi-client: multiple apps can connect simultaneously; status and connected IPs are shown in the Tools tab

docs.title: How-to: connect your phone app through the PC
docs.text:
Goal: the Meshtastic app on your phone shares the node attached to the PC — as if the client were a device of its own on the Wi-Fi.

  1. Prerequisite: the client is connected to the physical node; phone and PC are on the same network (Wi-Fi)
  2. Enable: Tools tab → tick "Enable Virtual Node" (default port 4404). The setting is persisted — from now on the server starts automatically whenever the client connects to the node. Optional: "Block admin commands from clients"
  3. Connect the phone: Meshtastic app → device selection → Network/TCP → enter the PC's IP address + port 4404 (find the IP via ipconfig; connected clients are listed in the Tools tab)
  4. Success check: the app immediately loads channels, node list and configuration; a test message from the phone shows up in the client — and vice versa
  5. Multiple devices: more apps can connect in parallel; the Tools tab shows status and IPs

Typical pitfalls:

  • App can't find the PC → Windows Firewall asks for permission on first start — allow it (or add an inbound rule for port 4404); also verify phone and PC really share the same Wi-Fi/subnet
  • Connected but no data → the client itself is not connected to the node right now; the order is client ↔ node, then phone ↔ client
  • Admin changes from the app don't apply → "Block admin commands from clients" is active (a locked kiosk mode blocks them additionally)
